full_text:
A young fawn was browsing in a peaceful forest clearing with his mother. Looking admiringly at his mother's graceful, slender limbs, sharp hooves, and keen ears, the young buck asked:

"Mother, why are you always so terrified of the dogs? You are much larger and swifter than they are; your hooves can deliver a crushing blow; you have sharp senses that detect danger miles away, and when I grow my antlers, we could easily pierce any hound. Why do you always flee at the first sound of their bark?"

The mother hind smiled tenderly and stroked her son's head:

"Every word you speak is the absolute truth, my child. I tell myself the very same things every single day: that I am swift, that I am large, and that I should stand my ground. But alas! The moment I hear the distant baying of a single hound echoing across the hills, all my courage evaporates in an instant, and my legs carry me away before I even know I am running!"
moral: No amount of logical reasoning can cure a heart ruled by inherited fear.

full_text:
A large brown bear loved to boast of his extraordinary gentleness, piety, and benevolence to all the woodland creatures. Standing before a gathering of animals, he puffed out his broad chest and declared:

"I am the most compassionate beast in all creation! Look at the lions, tigers, and wolves—how savagely they tear into living flesh! But as for me, I have such tender reverence for mortal life that I have never in all my years touched, harmed, or eaten a human corpse; I leave the departed to rest in peace!"

The other beasts nodded in polite admiration of his noble virtue. But the clever fox stepped forward, tilted his head, and remarked with a biting smile:

"Your piety would be far more convincing, Master Bear, if you showed the same tender mercy to the living that you show to the dead! You may spare the corpses who can feel no pain, but you slaughter the living with your claws without a single tremor of regret!"
moral: Hypocrisy that pretends to spare the dead while preying upon the living deserves no praise.

An ass found the skin of a lion left by hunters on the grass. Slipping his legs into the paws and pulling the massive mane over his head, he strutted through the countryside. Beasts and men fled in sheer terror before the apparition of the King of Beasts.

Exulting in his borrowed glory, the donkey encountered his master on the road. Wishing to terrify the man who had driven him with a stick, the ass opened his mouth to roar.

Out came a deafening, unmistakable bray: "HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!"

The master laughed heartily, grasped his stout hazel cudgel, and gave the disguised beast a sound thrashing across his ribs, saying: "You may frighten the sheep with that skin, you fool, but your ridiculous bray proves you are the same lazy donkey you have always been!"
moral: Pretending to be what you are not only invites mockery when your true nature appears.

title: The Horse and the Donkey
summary: A merchant set out for the city with his horse and donkey. The donkey was loaded to the brim with heavy merchandise, while the horse walked free, adorned with jingling bells....
full_text:
A merchant set out for the city with his horse and donkey. The donkey was loaded to the brim with heavy merchandise, while the horse walked free, adorned with jingling bells.

Halfway along the dusty mountain pass, the donkey faltered and pleaded: "Brother Horse, take but a small part of my load, or I shall die upon this path!"

The proud horse snorted and refused to soil his back. An hour later, the donkey dropped dead in the dust.

The merchant immediately took all the heavy baggage, the grain sacks, and the donkey's skin, and piled them entirely onto the back of the horse. Staggering under the crushing weight, the horse groaned: "By refusing to lift a small share, I must now bear the whole burden alone!"
moral: Help your fellow laborer in his time of trial, lest his burden fall upon your own shoulders.

title: The Stag at the Pool

full_text:
A stag came to a crystal pool to drink. Seeing his reflection in the calm water, he admired his magnificent, branching antlers with boundless pride, but felt deep shame at his slender, spindle legs.

"What a tragic contrast!" sighed the stag. "My majestic crown rivals a monarch's diadem, while my wretched legs are thin and weak."

Just then, the baying of hunting hounds and the shouts of hunters echoed through the woods. The stag sprang forward: his swift, slender legs carried him across the open plain like the wind, leaving the hounds far behind.

Entering the dense forest, his branching antlers caught tightly in the hanging branches of an oak. The hounds swarmed upon him. In his dying breath, the stag wept: "How blind I was! The legs I despised would have saved me, while the antlers I foolishly prized have brought my destruction!"
moral: We often despise the useful things that save us, and praise the ornamental vanity that brings ruin.

full_text:
A young fox who had never seen a lion encountered the King of Beasts on a woodland trail. The lion's thunderous stride and massive mane terrified the fox so utterly that he collapsed in the bushes, nearly dying of fright.

A month later, the fox met the lion a second time. He still felt deep dread, but this time he remained on his feet, hiding behind an oak tree and watching the great beast pass without trembling.

When they met for the third time, all fear had vanished from the fox's heart. He walked boldly up to the lion, tipped his hat, and engaged the King of the Forest in a polite, cheerful conversation about the weather, proving that understanding and experience conquer the terror of the unknown.
moral: Familiarity takes away the terrors of the unknown; courage grows through understanding.

full_text:
An ass trudging under heavy sacks of firewood met a magnificent warhorse bedecked with polished steel armor, flowing silk banners, and jingling silver bridles. The charger pranced proudly down the highway, demanding the lowly ass step aside into the ditch.

The humble ass envied the charger's royal treatment, his sweet oats, and his glorious status.

A few months later, the ass encountered the same horse being led slowly back from the battlefields. The charger's eye was blinded, his flank was scarred by spear thrusts, and he dragged a shattered leg behind him, dismissed to drag night-soil carts for the rest of his miserable days.

The ass looked upon his own sturdy legs and simple thistle meal, and thanked providence for his quiet, peaceful station in life, realizing that glorious ambition demands a terrible price.
moral: The glittering honors of high office carry mortal perils that humble peace escapes.

title: The Fox and the Bramble
summary: A fox, pursued closely by hounds, slipped as he leaped over a high garden hedge. Desperate to break his fall and save himself from the stony ravine below, he reached out and clampe...
full_text:
A fox, pursued closely by hounds, slipped as he leaped over a high garden hedge. Desperate to break his fall and save himself from the stony ravine below, he reached out and clamped his paws tightly around a dense wild bramble bush.

The sharp thorns pierced his tender pads, tearing his flesh and leaving him covered in blood. Howling in agony, the fox cried out:

"Cruel bush! I reached for you as a friend to save me from falling, and you have wounded me worse than the hounds!"

The bramble shook its thorny boughs and replied: "You were a fool to grasp me, neighbor Fox! Did you not know that it is my very nature to cling to and scratch everything that comes near me? Never expect gentle protection from that which lives by wounding others!"
moral: It is foolish to seek refuge in what is naturally armed to hurt whatever touches it.

title: The Snake and the File
summary: A venomous serpent slithered into a blacksmith's workshop in search of mice. Slithering across the workbench, his cold skin struck a heavy, hardened steel file used by the smith to...
full_text:
A venomous serpent slithered into a blacksmith's workshop in search of mice. Slithering across the workbench, his cold skin struck a heavy, hardened steel file used by the smith to sharpen iron tools.

Believing the file had struck him, the spiteful snake coiled in fury and sank his sharp fangs deep into the steel. He gnawed with venomous malice, determined to crush the stubborn object.

Presently, the serpent felt his mouth filling with warm liquid. Believing he had drawn blood from his foe, he bit harder and harder, until his fangs snapped, his gums were shredded to ribbons, and his jaws were ground away upon the hardened steel.

The lifeless file remained cold and intact, while the dying snake perished of his own blind malice, learning too late that futile rage against superior strength ruins only the aggressor.
moral: Never vent your malice against that which cannot be harmed, lest you destroy yourself.

full_text:
A lion strolling along the sea beach spotted a dolphin leaping gracefully through the waves. The lion called out to the sea creature:

"Noble Dolphin! You are sovereign of the deep waters, and I am King of the beasts of the earth. Let us enter into a royal alliance, swearing to assist each other whenever danger threatens!"

The dolphin agreed with joyous goodwill. Sometime later, the lion was engaged in a ferocious battle with a wild mountain bull near the water's edge. Being hard-pressed, the lion roared to his ally: "Help me, friend Dolphin! Fulfill your oath!"

The dolphin swam to the shallows, but could not crawl upon the dry sand to strike the bull. When the lion criticized him as a treacherous friend, the dolphin replied:

"Do not blame me, King Lion; blame Nature, who made me master of the ocean but gave me no feet to walk upon the shore. Do not demand help that lies outside your friend's natural power to give."
moral: An ally cannot help you beyond the natural sphere of his power.

full_text:
A country farmer had an old serpent living beneath his doorstep, which in a moment of fury bit his beloved son, killing the boy instantly. Overwhelmed by grief and rage, the farmer seized an axe, chased the serpent, and struck at its head; but the blow missed, merely severing the serpent's tail and leaving a deep gash in the rock.

Later, realizing that perpetual hatred brought no peace, the farmer placed bread and milk before the hole, seeking reconciliation.

The serpent poked its head out, gazed at the offered meal, and hissed sorrowfully:

"Farmer, take away your bread. There can never be true peace between us. So long as you look upon your child's grave, and so long as I look upon my severed tail and the deep scar in that rock, the memory of our injuries will poison every handshake."
moral: True reconciliation is impossible where monuments of mutual injury remain.

full_text:
A raven, observing a graceful swan gliding across a calm lake, became consumed with intense envy of the swan's dazzling white plumage. The raven concluded that the swan's snowy brilliance came solely from living in the clear water and washing its feathers every hour.

Abandoning his native woods, the raven took up residence in the marshes and lakes. From dawn to dusk, he bathed in the cold water, washing his feathers and rubbing his wings with river reeds.

He altered his diet to eat water weeds and pond moss instead of his natural food. But no amount of washing could lighten the pitch-black color of his feathers.

Within a month, unable to digest the watery marsh plants and chilled to the bone by constant immersion in the cold streams, the foolish raven grew weak and died of fever, proving that external habits cannot alter what nature has fundamentally designed.
moral: You cannot change your essential nature by altering your external environment.

full_text:
Two cooking pots—one fashioned of sturdy hammered brass, and the other made of delicate earthen clay—were swept from a kitchen shelf by a sudden flood and floated together down the swollen river.

The Brass Pot called out cheerfully to his clay companion: "Fear nothing, neighbor! Float close beside me; I will protect you and keep you safe from the crashing waves!"

The wise Earthen Pot paddled backward with all his might and replied:

"I thank you for your generous goodwill, friend, but I beg you to keep as far from me as possible! If a rock strikes me, I am shattered; but if you strike me in friendship, I am equally shattered to pieces. Whether we meet in battle or in friendly collision, the clay pot must always be the loser!"
moral: The weak must keep a safe distance from the strong; collision brings ruin to the fragile.

A young boy stole a hornbook from his schoolfellow and brought it home to his mother. Instead of correcting him, she praised his cleverness and patted his head. Encouraged by her approval, he stole a silver spoon from a neighbor, and she hid it with delight.

As the boy grew to manhood, his petty thefts expanded into violent highway robbery and murder. Eventually, he was captured by the king's soldiers and condemned to the gallows.

As he was led to the scaffold surrounded by a great crowd, his mother followed, weeping and tearing her hair. The condemned youth asked permission to whisper one last word in his mother's ear.

When she drew close, the youth clamped his teeth onto her earlobe and bit it clean off!

The crowd gasped in horror at the unnatural brutality. The youth turned to the crowd and cried with bitter tears: "Do not judge me alone! If this woman had struck my cheek when I first stole that little hornbook, I would not be standing beneath this gallows today; her praise has brought my ruin!"
moral: Neglecting to correct small faults in childhood breeds ruinous crimes in youth.

title: The Crab and His Mother
summary: An old mother crab sat on the sandy ocean shore, watching her young son scuttle sideways across the wet pebbles. Annoyed by his clumsy gait, she scolded him sharply:...
full_text:
An old mother crab sat on the sandy ocean shore, watching her young son scuttle sideways across the wet pebbles. Annoyed by his clumsy gait, she scolded him sharply:

"Why do you walk so crookedly, my child? It is disgraceful to shamble sideways through the sand! Turn your claws forward, straighten your shell, and walk in a straight, dignified line like a respectable citizen of the sea!"

The young crab bowed politely and replied:

"I should gladly walk straight, dear Mother, if you will only show me how! Walk forward yourself, and I will follow your footsteps with perfect obedience."

A cottager owned a marvelous hen that laid a shining egg of solid gold every single morning. The sale of these eggs brought the man and his household great comfort and ease.

Yet seeing his wealth accumulate gradually, an insatiable impatience seized his heart. He thought: "This bird must have a boundless mine of pure gold hidden inside her belly! Why should I wait day after day for a single egg? I will slaughter the hen and take the entire treasure at once!"

He killed the bird and cut her open, only to find her inside exactly like any common barnyard hen. He lost both his present wealth and his future fortune in a single stroke of blind greed.
moral: Covetous impatience destroys the golden gift of steady prosperity.

full_text:
An ass grazing in a meadow saw a ravenous wolf approaching with bared fangs. Knowing he had no speed to outrun the beast, the ass immediately began limping with dramatic groans, dragging his hind leg through the clover.

The curious wolf paused and asked: "Why do you limp so pitifully, beast?"

"Alas, sir," wept the ass, "while leaping a hedge, a giant, jagged thorn pierced the sole of my hoof! I know you are going to eat me, but I beg you: pull out the thorn first, lest it pierce your throat and choke you while you feast upon my flank!"

The wolf thought this prudent advice. He stepped behind the ass, lifted the hoof, and bent his eyes close to search for the thorn.

In that instant, the ass kicked out with both hind hooves with thunderous force! The iron-hard hooves struck the wolf squarely in the mouth, shattering his teeth and splitting his jaw, while the ass galloped off to safety, laughing at the fallen predator.
moral: Sharp presence of mind in danger turns an enemy’s weapons into his own downfall.

title: The Hart and the Vine

full_text:
A noble hart, pursued closely by hunters and baying hounds, plunged into a vineyard and concealed himself beneath the dense, broad leaves of an ancient grapevine. The hunters rode past the arbor without noticing him, and the danger receded into the distance.

Feeling safe and hungry, the foolish hart began to nibble and strip the very vine leaves that had sheltered him from death.

The rustling of the stripped foliage and the snapping of branches caught the ears of the returning hunters. Turning around, they saw the tips of his antlers through the ruined canopy. An arrow was notched, and the hart was pierced to the heart.

Dying upon the soil, he groaned in bitter regret: "I suffer justice! I should have cherished the vine that preserved my life, rather than destroying my savior for a mouthful of green food."
moral: He who destroys the shelter that saved him pays for his ingratitude with his life.

A hungry lion pacing below a sheer limestone precipice looked up and saw a nimble mountain goat browsing sweet thyme upon a high crag.

The lion called out with sweet, coaxing words: "Come down, fair goat! The rocks above are steep and perilous; you might slip and fall. The meadow down here is full of clover, cool brooks, and rich grass!"

The goat looked down from her secure perch and replied: "The grass below may be sweet, Master Lion, but you invite me down not that I may dine upon your meadows, but that you may dine upon me!"
moral: Beware the friendly invitations of predators whose interest is their own belly.

An ass noticed how tenderly his master pampered a tiny lapdog: the little dog was fed choice meat from the table, carried in the master's arms, and kissed affectionately whenever it leaped onto his lap and wagged its tail.

The ass thought: "If I act playful and affectionate like that little creature, the master will love me too and feed me sweets instead of dry straw!"

Breaking from his halter, the clumsy ass galloped into the dining parlor, kicked over the tea table, brayed loudly, and leaped with his heavy hooves straight onto the master's chest, licking his face with a rough, slobbery tongue!

Terrified by the assault, the master shouted for help. The servants rushed in with heavy staves and gave the clumsy ass such a merciless thrashing that he barely crawled back to his stable, realizing that an ass can never play the part of a lapdog.
moral: Do not attempt to ape manners that nature never intended for you.

full_text:
A celebrated city buffoon drew immense crowds to the theater by mimicking the squealing of a pig beneath his cloak. He squeaked, grunted, and squealed so humorously that the audience cheered and awarded him the grand prize.

A simple countryman in the crowd stood up and declared that he would compete against the buffoon the following evening.

The next day, the theater was packed. The buffoon repeated his performance and received thunderous applause.

The countryman then stepped onto the stage, wrapped in a thick cloak. He pinched a real live piglet concealed beneath his arm, causing the animal to squeal and shriek with genuine pig cries.

The audience jeered and hissed, throwing rotten fruit and shouting: "Terrible! The buffoon sounds far more like a pig than you do!"

The countryman pulled the live piglet out from under his cloak and held it high above his head: "Behold, critics! It is not me you are hissing, but the pig himself! Your prejudice prefers a counterfeit to nature's own truth!"
moral: Prejudice blinds men to genuine truth in favor of celebrated counterfeits.

Infuriated by the insect's insolence, the man swung his palm with tremendous force to crush the offender. But the nimble fly buzzed away unhurt, while the man's own hand struck his bare skull with a loud, stinging SLAP that left his ears ringing.

The fly landed again upon his nose and mocked: "You wished to avenge a tiny bite with death; now what have you gained by your own furious blow?"

The man rubbed his aching brow and replied: "I am easily reconciled with myself, for I intended no malice to my own head; but you, contemptible creature that lives only to torment others, I would gladly suffer a hundred blows to crush!"
moral: Uncontrolled rage at petty irritations causes more self-inflicted harm than the offense.

A merchant whose ship was shattered in a terrible storm managed to drag himself onto the sandy shore, barely escaping drowning. Exhausted and bitter at the loss of all his cargo, he sat upon the beach and cursed the Sea, calling her treacherous, merciless, and a trap for mankind.

The Sea took the form of a majestic woman rising from the foam and addressed the weeping mariner:

"Do not lay the blame for your ruin at my door, wanderer! Look upon me: of my own nature, I am calm, tranquil, and clear as glass, gently bearing ships upon my breast. It is the violent Winds that fall upon me with fury, stirring my waters into mountains of foam and driving ships onto rocks. Blame the storms that incite the strife, not the calm element that is stirred against its will!"
moral: Do not blame the instrument for the violence of the tempest that stirs it.

A mule, fed abundantly on rich oats and barley, grew fat, glossy, and puffed up with boundless conceit. He galloped across the pasture, kicking up his heels and neighing:

"My father was a royal racehorse, swifter than the wind! I have inherited his noble blood, his speed, and his magnificent stature!"

He galloped around the meadow, trying to outrun the wind. But after half a mile, his breath failed, his knees trembled, and he slowed to a plodding, stubborn walk.

Remembering his limitations, he sighed in humility: "Alas, my memory was too short: I remembered my father the racehorse, but I entirely forgot my mother the common donkey!"
moral: Pride in noble ancestry is swiftly humbled when the full heritage is remembered.

Presently, a hunter appeared with arrows and hounds. The stag bounded away: his slender legs carried him across the open plain with breathless speed, saving him from the arrows.

Entering a dense thicket, his spreading horns became entangled in the brambles and branches. Held fast, the hounds overtook him.

As he fell beneath their claws, he cried: "Unhappy creature that I am! The legs I despised were my salvation, while the antlers I loved have brought my doom!"
moral: True value often lies in what is humble, while proud adornments bring peril.

As the peasant lifted the horn to his parched lips, the grateful eagle swooped from the clouds, struck the poisoned vessel from the man's hands with his wing, and shattered it upon the rocks, saving his deliverer's life and repaying kindness with loyalty.
moral: An act of kindness shown to the helpless returns as a shield in mortal peril.

A little kid goat stood upon the high thatched roof of a sheepcote, looking down at a wolf passing by the fence below. Feeling completely secure behind the high walls, the little goat began shouting insults, sticking out his tongue, and mocking the predator's gray fur and wicked eyes.

The wolf paused, looked up calmly at the insolent little creature, and replied:

"Taunt on, little fool! It is not you who reviles me, but the sturdy roof and high wall upon which you stand! Take away the stone beneath your hooves, and we would see how brave your tongue would be!"
moral: Cowardly taunts from a place of safety show no real valor; it is the wall that speaks.

full_text:
The oxen of the land assembled in a vast herd to plan a war of extermination against the butchers, who slaughtered their kind daily. They sharpened their horns and prepared to stampede upon the city.

A wise old ox, who had plowed the fields for many seasons, stepped forward and addressed the herd:

"Pause, brothers, and consider! The butchers slaughter us with practiced hands and sharp blades, ending our lives with swiftness. But if we destroy the butchers, men will still eat beef, and they will employ clumsy, inexperienced laborers who will hack us to pieces with dull axes, prolonging our agony tenfold! Better to endure the skilled master than suffer under the ignorant amateur!"
moral: Beware lest in destroying a known evil you invite an untried and harsher calamity.

full_text:
A lion and a bear found a slain fawn in the forest at the exact same moment. Both claimed the prize, and neither would yield a single scrap to the other.

They engaged in a terrible duel: teeth clashed against claws, blood flowed, and they tore each other until both collapsed upon the grass, bruised, bleeding, and too exhausted to lift a paw or move a muscle.

A fox, who had been watching the battle from behind a bush, trotted casually into the clearing. Seeing both titans incapacitated, he picked up the fawn between his jaws and walked off into the thicket at his leisure.

The dying fighters watched him depart, sighing in bitter sorrow: "How tragic our folly! We tore each other to pieces, only that a cowardly rogue might feast upon the fruit of our toil!"
moral: When two mighty contenders tear each other apart, a cunning onlooker steals the prize.

full_text:
A wolf began following a shepherd and his flock from a respectful distance. He never attacked a sheep, never bared his fangs, and even helped turn back stragglers that wandered toward the ravine.

Gradually, the shepherd grew accustomed to the wolf's quiet presence, regarding him as a faithful second hound.

One afternoon, needing to run an urgent errand in the town, the shepherd left his entire flock under the sole guardianship of the quiet wolf.

The moment the shepherd vanished over the hill, the wolf gave a savage howl, attacked the flock with ravenous ferocity, and slaughtered half the sheep before the sun set.

Returning to the carnage, the weeping shepherd beat his breast: "I suffer justice! What madness possessed me to entrust sheep to the custody of a wolf?"
moral: Trusting a natural predator to guard the flock is an invitation to slaughter.

full_text:
The hares were living in constant terror of hunters, dogs, eagles, and wild beasts. Grieving over their perpetual anxiety and trembling lives, they held a solemn assembly and resolved to end their misery together by leaping into a deep mountain lake.

As the herd of hares galloped toward the water's edge to drown themselves, a colony of frogs sitting on the bank took fright at the thundering footsteps and plunged into the muddy depths in wild panic.

A wise old hare stopped the procession, shouting:

"Halt, brothers! See those frogs? They tremble before our footsteps as we tremble before the hounds! We are not the most miserable of creatures on earth; take heart and live on!"
moral: However heavy your afflictions seem, there are always others who endure greater trials.

title: The Fox and the Woodcutter
summary: A fox, breathless and exhausted from a long pursuit by royal hounds, burst into a clearing where an honest woodcutter was chopping pine logs. The fox fell upon his knees and begged...
full_text:
A fox, breathless and exhausted from a long pursuit by royal hounds, burst into a clearing where an honest woodcutter was chopping pine logs. The fox fell upon his knees and begged: "Have mercy, woodcutter! Hide me in your cottage, I implore you, or the hounds will tear me apart!"

The woodcutter pointed toward his rustic hut and promised to protect him. The fox dashed inside and crouched beneath a pile of dry faggots.

A moment later, the huntsmen arrived on foaming horses. "Woodcutter!" shouted the captain. "Did a fox pass this way?"

"No, I have seen no fox!" shouted the woodcutter with a loud, honest voice. But at the very same moment, he slyly pointed his thumb toward the door of his cottage, winking at the hunters.

The huntsmen, listening only to his words and ignoring his gesture, galloped past down the road.

When the danger had passed, the fox emerged from the hut and trotted off into the woods without uttering a single word of thanks.

"Where is your gratitude?" called the woodcutter indignantly. "I saved your skin, and you leave without a polite farewell!"

The fox turned around and replied: "I would have thanked you with all my heart if your fingers had agreed with your tongue, and if your deeds had not contradicted your speech!"
moral: Hypocrisy that swears faith with words while betraying with deeds is contemptible.

title: The Birdcatcher and the Lark
summary: A birdcatcher was busily spreading fine horsehair nets across a stubble field and scattering sweet millet seeds upon the ground to entice woodland birds....
full_text:
A birdcatcher was busily spreading fine horsehair nets across a stubble field and scattering sweet millet seeds upon the ground to entice woodland birds.

A crest-lark perched upon a wild rose bush watched him from afar and asked curiously: "Good sir, what magnificent work are you engaged in with those ropes and pegs?"

The birdcatcher smiled warmly and replied: "I am laying the foundations of a grand, prosperous new city where all creatures may live in abundance and peace!"

With these words, the man retreated into the bushes.

The simple lark, captivated by the promise of a peaceful city and enticed by the scattered grain, fluttered down to feast. The moment his claws touched the seed, the snare snapped shut, tangling his delicate wings in the horsehair cords.

As the birdcatcher stepped forward to wring his neck, the lark wept in bitter despair: "Alas! If this is the kind of city you build, master builder, you will find very few citizens willing to inhabit it!"
moral: Beware the treacherous stranger who lays traps while pretending to build a city.

full_text:
An elderly fisherman sat upon a stone pier casting his line into the sea all morning without success. At noon, his cork bobbed under, and he pulled up a tiny sprat no bigger than his thumb.

As the fisherman prepared to toss the tiny catch into his willow basket, the little fish opened his mouth and gasped:

"Have pity, fisherman! Look at how small I am—I am barely a single bite for a hungry man! Throw me back into the cool ocean waves! Let me swim and grow fat for another season; then you may catch me again and sell me at the harbor market for a silver coin!"

The old fisherman slipped the little fish into his creel, secured the wicker lid, and replied with a serene smile:

"I should be a fool indeed to surrender a small fish already in my basket on the doubtful chance of catching a larger one in the stormy future!"
moral: A small certainty in hand is worth far more than a grand promise in the future.

title: The Shepherd and the Sheep

full_text:
A shepherd driving his flock into the sheepfold grew impatient when the sheep clustered at the narrow gate. He began shouting harshly, throwing stones, and setting his fierce dog upon the gentle creatures, tearing their soft fleeces.

An elderly bell-wether paused in the gateway, turned his curling horns toward the shepherd, and spoke with gentle dignity:

"Why do you treat us so roughly, master? We yield you rich milk to drink every morning; we surrender our soft wool each spring to keep you warm through winter storms; and we follow your pipe across the hills without complaint. If you treat those who give you everything with violence, how will you treat your enemies?"

Ashamed of his harsh temper, the shepherd called off his hound and guided the gentle flock with patient care.
moral: Those who yield their gifts peacefully deserve gentle and patient treatment.

full_text:
An elderly woman, who had enjoyed fine vintage Falernian wine in her youth, came across an ancient earthenware amphora lying in an abandoned cellar.

The jar was completely empty; not a single drop of wine remained within its earthen belly. Yet the clay had absorbed the rich spirit for so many decades that when she leaned over the rim and inhaled deeply, the fragrance of sweet grapes, oak, and honey filled her senses.

Closing her eyes with nostalgic delight, the old woman murmured:

"Ah, what an exquisite vessel! How marvelous must have been the liquor that once filled your heart, when even your empty dregs leave behind such a heavenly fragrance!"
moral: The lingering fragrance of past excellence reveals how noble the original virtue was.

full_text:
A man and a lion were traveling together down a highway, debating which of their kinds possessed superior strength, nobility, and courage.

As they entered a public square in a grand city, the man pointed triumphantly to a colossal marble statue depicting a heroic huntsman standing victorious over a slain lion, pinning the beast beneath his heel.

"See there!" exclaimed the man in boasting pride. "Look at that monument! Does that not prove beyond dispute that man is mightier than the lion?"

The lion smiled calmly, flicked his tail, and replied:

"If lions knew how to carve stone statues as men do, friend, you would see a hundred monuments showing one lion tearing ten huntsmen to shreds!"
moral: History is written by the narrator; perspective changes when both sides tell the tale.

moral: Those who maliciously destroy the fruit of the earth will face righteous retribution.

moral: Physician, heal thyself before you presume to cure the infirmities of others.

moral: Discord among allies is the open door through which enemies enter to devour.

The lazy wagoner dropped his whip, fell to his knees in the mud, and began praying loudly to the heroic champion Hercules to come down from the clouds and lift his wagon.

A voice of thunder echoed from the heavens:

"Take up your whip, idle knave! Put your shoulder to the wheel and urge your team forward! How do you expect assistance when you refuse to lift a single finger to help yourself?"
moral: Heaven helps those who put their own shoulder to the wheel.

full_text:
A farmer spread nets across his newly sown wheat fields to catch the destructive cranes and geese that were devouring his seed.

When he inspected his nets, he found several cranes and one gentle, harmless Stork caught in the mesh.

The Stork pleaded: "Spare me, farmer! I am no crane; I am a pious stork, dutiful to my parents and eating only frogs and insects!"

The farmer replied: "That may be true, but you were caught in the company of the thieves who destroy my harvest, and you must suffer the same fate as your companions!"
moral: Those who keep company with thieves share in the punishment of the crime.

A traveler hired a donkey and driver to carry him across a parched desert on a blistering afternoon. Seeking relief from the scorching sun, the traveler sat down in the donkey's shadow.

The driver objected: "You hired the donkey, not his shadow! If you want the shadow, you must pay extra!"

They argued passionately, while the donkey, tired of the shouting, kicked up his heels and trotted away into the desert, leaving both men stranded under the scorching sun without donkey or shadow.
moral: Quarreling over shadows loses the real substance of the journey.

full_text:
A woodman walked into an ancient forest and begged the trees to grant him a single piece of hardwood to fashion a handle for his iron axe head.

The noble oak and pine trees took pity on him and graciously gave him a branch of plain ash wood.

The woodman fitted the handle to his axe and immediately began cutting down the magnificent oaks, pines, and beeches, laying the forest bare.

The dying oak wept to the cedar: "Our own foolish charity provided the weapon that destroys us all!"
moral: Giving your enemy the means to hurt your brother leads swiftly to your own destruction.

full_text:
On a freezing winter morning, a farmer found a venomous viper stiff with frost, dying on the snow. Touched with compassion, the man picked up the frozen creature and placed it inside his warm coat.

Revived by the warmth of the farmer's breast, the serpent regained its strength and immediately sank its poisonous fangs deep into the farmer's flesh.

Dying upon the snow, the farmer groaned in bitter remorse: "I suffer justice for having shown mercy to a creature whose very nature is venomous ingratitude!"
moral: Kindness shown to the venomous and ungrateful is repaid with a deadly sting.

full_text:
A cunning cat crept into a barn and seized a rooster, seeking an excuse to devour him with a show of justice. "You disturb honest folks," hissed the cat, "crowing in the dead of night and waking laborers from their sleep!"

The cock replied: "I crow for their benefit, alerting them that dawn is near so they may begin honest toil."

"Be that as it may," snarled the cat, "you are an unnatural rogue who respects no family ties!"

"I do that only that hens may lay fertile eggs for our master's table," reasoned the cock.

The cat bared her claws: "Though your arguments are clever, I will not go without my breakfast!" and devoured him on the spot.
moral: A tyrant determined upon cruelty will always invent a hypocritical excuse.

An ass, enchanted by the chirping melodies of grasshoppers in the meadow, asked them: "What sweet nectar do you eat that gives you such musical voices?"

"We feed only upon morning dew," they chirped in jest.

The gullible ass resolved to eat nothing but dew. He grazed no grass, ate no thistles, and licked only dew from the morning leaves. Within two weeks, the foolish beast starved to death, proving that you cannot adopt another's diet without destroying your own life.
moral: Attempting to change your nature to imitate others brings only starvation.

A lion found a sleeping hare in the brush and was about to devour her when a magnificent stag bounded past. The greedy lion abandoned the sleeping hare to chase the stag through the rocks.

After a long, exhausting chase, the swift stag escaped into the mountains. The panting lion returned to the thicket to eat the hare, only to find she had awakened and scampered away.

The hungry lion sighed: "I deserve this empty belly; I abandoned a certain meal in hand to chase an elusive phantom!"
moral: He who grasps at a larger prize in the distance loses what is already in his grasp.

A wolf passing an oat field found heavy sheaves of ripe oats. Being a carnivore, he could not eat grain, so he invited a grazing horse to the feast, boasting of his boundless generosity.

The horse smiled calmly and replied:

moral: Never trust an enemy who offers you benefits he cannot consume himself.

full_text:
A veteran hunting hound, who had tackled fierce boars and stags in his youth, seized a wild boar by the ear. But his worn teeth slipped from the animal's hide, and the prey escaped.

His ungrateful master ran up and struck the old dog with his whip.

The bleeding hound looked up with sorrowful eyes: "Master, my heart was willing, but my strength has failed with age. Praise me for what I have accomplished in your service, rather than beating me because my youth has departed!"
moral: Honor past service; do not reproach an old servant whose strength fails after years of devotion.

full_text:
Two travelers swore mutual defense against all perils. Entering a forest, a giant bear charged out of the brush.

One traveler scrambled up a tall tree, thinking only of himself. The other, unable to climb, threw himself flat upon the ground, holding his breath and feigning death, for bears touch no corpse.

The bear sniffed his ears, nose, and lips, and lumbered away into the hills.

The man in the tree climbed down and asked with a laugh: "What did the bear whisper in your ear?"

"He gave me sound advice," replied the companion: "never travel with a comrade who deserts you in the hour of danger!"
moral: Adversity tests the sincerity of friendship.

A hunter armed with bows and spears walked through the forest, loudly boasting that he was searching for a lion to slay.

Meeting a woodman, the hunter asked: "Have you seen any lion's tracks in this valley?"

The woodman replied: "I can do better than show you his tracks; I will lead you straight to the cave where the lion is sleeping!"

The hunter turned pale, his teeth chattering in terror: "No, no! I was looking only for his tracks, not for the beast himself!" and he sprinted down the mountain path in panic.
moral: The boaster is brave in search of the track, but terrified when the beast appears.

full_text:
A wild horse had a bitter feud with a stag over grazing territory. Desiring revenge, the horse asked a man to help him hunt down the stag.

The man agreed on one condition: the horse must accept an iron bit in his mouth and a leather saddle on his back.

With the man on his back, the horse easily ran down and killed the stag. But when the horse asked to be set free, the man laughed, hitched him to a stable post, and rode him as a beast of burden for the rest of his days.
moral: He who sells his liberty to avenge an insult becomes a perpetual slave.

full_text:
A goatherd sheltered his flock in a cave during a winter storm, finding several wild goats inside. Wishing to entice the wild herd into his own flock, he fed them sweet corn, while starving his own faithful goats on dry chaff.

When the storm passed, the wild goats galloped away into the mountains.

"Ungrateful beasts!" shouted the goatherd. "I fed you choice corn, and you desert me!"

A wild goat called back: "We flee precisely because you favored us above your own flock; if new goats arrived tomorrow, you would neglect us in turn!"
moral: Do not neglect old friends to curry favor with untried strangers.

moral: Never minister to the requests of a predator whose recovery means your slaughter.

moral: Grasp difficult tasks with bold resolution; timid hesitation brings stinging pain.

moral: Beware the man who blows hot and cold with the same breath.

A fox fell into a deep well and could not climb the sheer walls. A thirsty goat approached and asked if the water was good.

The fox praised the sweet taste of the water, urging the goat to jump down.

The foolish goat leaped in and drank her fill. The fox then placed his forepaws upon the goat's long horns, sprang nimbly out of the well, and looked down from the rim.

When the trapped goat cried for help, the fox called back: "Had you as much sense in your skull as you have hairs on your chin, you would have looked for a way out before leaping into the pit!"
moral: Look before you leap; consider the exit before you enter into an undertaking.

While she was away gathering fish, a violent ocean storm arose. Towering tidal waves swept up the rock face, smashing her nest and drowning her fledglings.

Returning to the ruins, the grief-stricken bird wept: "In fleeing the perils of the land, I sought refuge with the sea, and the ocean has proved far more merciless than the earth!"
moral: In fleeing perils of the land, beware lest you build your nest where the waves can reach.

A house dog invited a stray dog to attend his master's grand banquet. The stray entered the kitchen, admiring the roasts and anticipating a feast.

The master cook, seeing a strange cur wagging his tail in the pantry, seized the dog by the hind legs and hurled him through the open window into the cobblestone courtyard.

Limping home bruised and starving, the stray told his companions: "The feast was so magnificent that I drank so much wine I cannot even remember how I left the house!"
moral: Never attend an entertainment upon an invitation from one who owns neither house nor dinner.

moral: Treachery against an ally invites righteous retribution from above.

title: The Eagle and the Beetle

full_text:
A hare fled from an eagle and sought refuge with a humble dung beetle. The beetle pleaded for the hare's life, but the haughty eagle struck the beetle aside with her wing and devoured the hare.

The beetle sought revenge: whenever the eagle laid eggs in high nests, the beetle flew up and rolled the eggs out, smashing them upon the rocks.

Even when the eagle laid her eggs in the lap of the celestial ruler, the beetle dropped a pellet of dirt, causing the sovereign to rise and accidentally smash the eggs, proving that contempt for the weak brings inescapable justice.
moral: Never despise the smallest enemy when justice is on his side.

title: The Ass and the Dog
summary: A traveler slept beneath an oak while his ass grazed and his dog starved. The dog begged the ass for a crust from the master's pannier, but the ass refused....
full_text:
A traveler slept beneath an oak while his ass grazed and his dog starved. The dog begged the ass for a crust from the master's pannier, but the ass refused.

Presently, a wolf approached. The terrified ass called upon the dog to protect him.

The dog lay down and replied: "Wait until the master wakes, as you told me to wait for my dinner!" and the wolf brought the ass down.
moral: He who refuses bread to his companion is deserted in the hour of peril.

title: The Boasting Traveler

full_text:
A traveler returned from abroad boasting that while in Rhodes, he had leaped a distance greater than any Olympic champion, calling upon the citizens of Rhodes to verify his claim.

A listener stepped forward and said: "Friend, we do not need witnesses from Rhodes! Imagine that this very field is Rhodes: here is Rhodes, now leap here!"

The boaster turned pale and slunk away, unable to demonstrate at home what he claimed to have accomplished abroad.
moral: Do not boast of distant deeds; demonstrate your prowess here and now.

title: The Two Bags
summary: Every mortal is born carrying two bags: one hanging before his chest, and the other hanging behind his back....
full_text:
Every mortal is born carrying two bags: one hanging before his chest, and the other hanging behind his back.

The bag in front is filled with the faults, sins, and blunders of his neighbors; this bag is constantly before his eyes, examined with critical relish.

The bag behind his back contains his own grievous faults, hidden from his view and forgotten.

Thus it is that men spend their lives condemning the small errors of others while remaining completely blind to the heavy sins that crush their own shoulders.
moral: Men see the faults of others before their eyes, while blind to their own behind their backs.

A farmer was snowbound in his remote cottage during a fierce winter blizzard. Cut off from town and provisions, he first slaughtered his sheep for food.

When the snow continued, he slaughtered his goats, and then his plowing oxen.

Seeing the oxen killed, his faithful watchdogs looked at one another and said: "Let us fly into the storm! If our master has butchered his working oxen who plowed his bread, he will certainly make short work of us next!"
moral: When a master begins to devour his own household, it is time for the servants to fly.

An evergreen olive tree mocked a fig tree for shedding her leaves in autumn: "Look at you, bare and naked, while my leaves remain green all year round!"

moral: Boasting of green leaves invites the heavy snow that snaps proud branches.

title: The Frogs Complaining Against the Sun

full_text:
When the Sun announced his marriage, mortals celebrated, but the frogs in the marsh began croaking in mournful protest.

Asked why they lamented, an old frog answered: "One sun alone dries up our pools and bakes our marshes into dust; if he marries and begets sons, all the waters on earth will vanish and we shall perish!"
moral: Beware lest the marriage of one tyrant multiplies your oppressors tenfold.

title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
summary: A lark nested in a ripe wheat field. Hearing the farmer say he would ask his neighbors to help reap, the wise mother told her chicks not to worry....
full_text:
A lark nested in a ripe wheat field. Hearing the farmer say he would ask his neighbors to help reap, the wise mother told her chicks not to worry.

When the farmer said he would ask his cousins, she still stayed calm.

Finally, the farmer said: "Tomorrow I will take my sickle and cut the wheat myself!"

"Now it is time to fly!" said the mother lark. "When a man resolves to do his own work, the harvest will truly begin!"
moral: If you want a thing done, do it yourself; do not depend upon neighbors or kin.

title: The Lion, the Fox, and the Stag
summary: A sick lion used a fox to entice a stag into his cave. The lion struck, clipping the stag's ear, and the prey fled....
full_text:
A sick lion used a fox to entice a stag into his cave. The lion struck, clipping the stag's ear, and the prey fled.

The fox persuaded the foolish stag to return. The lion killed the stag, and the fox stole the brain.

When the lion asked for the brain, the fox replied: "A creature that returned twice into a lion's den had no brains in his skull!"
moral: He who falls twice into the same trap has no brains in his head.

title: The Fowler and the Ringdove
summary: A fowler took his reed limed with bird-lime and went out into the woods to snare ringdoves. Spotting a beautiful dove perched in a tall tree, he stood beneath the boughs, raised hi...
full_text:
A fowler took his reed limed with bird-lime and went out into the woods to snare ringdoves. Spotting a beautiful dove perched in a tall tree, he stood beneath the boughs, raised his rod, and aimed carefully.

While his eyes were fixed on the sky, he stepped backward and trod upon an adder sleeping in the grass.

The viper struck his heel with deadly venom. Dying upon the earth, the fowler gasped: "While I sought to bring down a harmless bird from the air, death struck me from beneath my feet!"
moral: He who plots death against the innocent often treads upon his own doom.

title: The Ass and the Grasshoppers Wisdom
summary: An ass admired the music of grasshoppers and asked what they ate to sing so sweetly....
full_text:
An ass admired the music of grasshoppers and asked what they ate to sing so sweetly.

The insects told him they drank only dew. The ass stopped eating grain and clover, licking only morning dew from the leaves until he perished of starvation, proving that imitation of another's nature brings ruin.
moral: Desiring another’s natural gifts without their constitution brings starvation.
